summary:
Kogi State stands under Nigeria's national framework. The Same Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act was passed by the House of Representatives on 30 May 2013 and signed into law by President Goodluck Jonathan in January 2014; entering a same-sex marriage or civil union carries 14 years' imprisonment, and registering, operating or participating in gay clubs, societies and organisations, or making a public show of a same-sex amorous relationship, carries 10 years.

Human Rights Watch (October 2016) records that the Act additionally bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, and that police have used it to justify torture and arbitrary arrests; the penalties it sets run from 10 to 14 years' imprisonment.

The Criminal Code applies separately in Kogi, criminalising sex between men with up to 14 years' imprisonment and gross indecency with up to 3 years. The twelve Shari'a-administering northern states impose harsher penalties, with death penalties applied in Kano and Katsina for lesbianism; non-Shari'a states such as Kogi sit under the 14-year national maximum instead.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Nigeria (June 2025, updated April 2026) assesses that same-sex sex between men is criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment, and that Shari'a law in all twelve northern states criminalises same-sex acts between men and between women, with male sodomy carrying the death penalty under state Zina provisions.

Official foreign travel guidance aimed at LGBT+ visitors is explicit and current. Sahara Reporters (19 August 2026), reporting the UK FCDO's updated Nigeria travel advice, relays warnings of arrest, violence, attacks, blackmail and intimidation against LGBT+ travellers; same-sex activity is illegal with up to 14 years' imprisonment; some northern states under Shari'a law can prescribe the death penalty; and the Same Sex Marriage Prohibition Act also reaches helpers and attendees of same-sex weddings.

A 2022 ruling by a coalition of Nigerian human rights organisations held that Sections 4(1), 5(2) and 5(3) of the 2013 Act breached the Constitution and could not be enforced anywhere in the country, effectively allowing LGBTQ+ organisations and individuals to exist and organise. No comparable ruling is recorded for the conduct-prohibition or marriage-prohibition provisions, which remain in force.

The Constitution contains no specific protections on sexual orientation, and there are no federal anti-discrimination protections for LGBTQ people.

Trans visitors face lethal violence. The beaten body of the Abuja trans TikToker 'Abuja Area Mama', a 33-year-old transgender woman, was found on a highway in Abuja in August 2024; BBC News (9 August 2024) reports that police opened an investigation, that she had been stabbed a year earlier, and that she had feared for her life. Mass arrests and detention of LGBTQ+ people are common across Nigeria, including in Kogi, and are especially frequent in northern states.
tangentialFactors:
The death penalty for same-sex conduct applies only under Shari'a provisions in twelve northern states, not in Kogi; the practical exposure in Kogi is the 14-year national maximum, the 10-year organisation and public-display provisions, and the 3-year gross-indecency penalty under the Criminal Code.

Enforcement across Nigeria takes the form of mass arrests and detention of LGBTQ+ people rather than isolated prosecutions, a pattern the BBC records as common nationwide and especially frequent in northern states. Kogi is named as one of the states where such arrests and detentions occur.

Foreign governments treat Nigeria as a country where LGBT+ travellers face arrest, violence, attacks, blackmail and intimidation, and where the 2014 statute extends beyond couples to helpers and attendees at same-sex weddings. That guidance is aimed at visitors generally and is not specific to Kogi.
localsOnly:
The 2022 court ruling on Sections 4(1), 5(2) and 5(3) of the Same Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act applies nationwide, including in Kogi: those provisions were held to breach the Constitution and cannot be enforced, which is what allows LGBTQ+ organisations and individuals to exist and register without facing the 10-year organisation offences.

The conduct and marriage provisions of the Act were not covered by that ruling and remain enforceable, as do the Criminal Code offences of sex between men (up to 14 years) and gross indecency (up to 3 years).

Residents have no constitutional protection based on sexual orientation and no federal anti-discrimination protection; police have used the Act to justify torture and arbitrary arrests, per Human Rights Watch.

Mass arrests and detention of LGBTQ+ people occur in Kogi as elsewhere in Nigeria, with the highest frequency recorded in northern states.
outOfScopeNotes:
Human Rights Watch's Nigeria country page yielded no usable finding for this record beyond the 2016 report cited in the parent framework; it is not separately relied on here.

Whether the 2022 ruling has been invoked against prosecutions in Kogi is not sourced in the inventory and remains unresolved. The inventory also gives no Kogi-specific arrest dates, charge outcomes or detention figures, only the general BBC finding that such arrests occur there.

How the 10-year organisation offences and the 14-year marriage offence are charged after the 2022 ruling, given that only Sections 4(1), 5(2) and 5(3) were struck down, is not resolved by the available sources.

The Wikipedia entry is the source for the statutory dates, penalty ranges, the Shari'a comparison and the 2022 ruling; those specifics are not corroborated here by primary legislation or a judgment text.
